articles.title: Worshipwrecked: Maha’s favourite is now the GaneshOTTsav
articles.summary: So we once more bade farewell to our beloved Ganeshji.
articles.body: So we once more bade farewell to our beloved Ganeshji. But the welcoming shouts of ‘Ganpati Bappa aala’ soon sounded like the swinging ’50s chartbuster, ‘(Ganpati) Be Bop-pa-Lula’. There even seemed to be more dancing Ganeshas than usual, but Maharashtra’s fave deity might well have swapped his father’s serene ‘Nataraja’ pose and done a tandava. Worship was more like warship: mandals-pandals battled to have the tallest idol bedecked most extravagantly from crown to toe-ring, gaudiest décor, loudest surround sound, and even more jarring neta-mugshot posters. Naturally the biggest fight was over big-ticket sponsors, who themselves competed to feed and feed off the blessing economy. So, the lusty cry was again ‘Ganpati Bappa More-ya’. All this for a deity who needs only a simple modak, a red hibiscus, and 21 blades of durva grass.Vighnaharta surely had problems negotiating the obstacles to genuine devotion. He must have even lost his head. You could almost hear him grumble, ‘It’s majha utsav, na, but it has become crass entertainment for my so-called celebrants.’Then Ashtavinayak listed his eight grievances:l My Mahadev-pita was covered only with ash but I have to be covered by insurance – for all my jewellery rivalling an AA-grade wedding.l Do you think my blessings are weighed against the gold chains you offer? How thick can you be?’l Bappa re, you seriously expect me to stomach sugar-free modak?l At the raja of pandals, aarti was full chamak-dhamak Bollywood. Laser-vazer, dry-ice smoke machines, drones raining confetti, a chorus in coordinated costumes, clapping theatrically for the cameras, with no shred of sincere ‘Namo-namaha’.l Crowds jostled as much for film-star darshan.l VIP queues for Tilak’s sarvajanik Ganeshotsav.l And deejay-sheejays at visarjan. They were dhoom machaoing in their own dhoon. CM tried banning them, but who will decibel the voter-catch?l Some of the speaker stacks towered higher than my mangal-murti, thumping out the racket for miles.Seemed like the massed shout asking me to return quickly next year, Pudhchya varshi laukarya, was more Pudhchya varshi louder-karu-ya!Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: Chandigarh's Neerja Bhanot in 1986, Mumbai's Smit Machchhar in 2026: 40 years apart, 2 attacks mid-air, 2 heroes who put passengers before themselves
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Four decades apart, two aviation professionals found themselves at the centre of terrifying emergencies in the skies, and both put the safety
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Four decades apart, two aviation professionals found themselves at the centre of terrifying emergencies in the skies, and both put the safety of passengers ahead of their own.In 1986, Chandigarh-born flight attendant Neerja Bhanot became a symbol of courage when she helped passengers escape from the hijacked Pan Am Flight 73 at Karachi before being fatally shot by the terrorists.In 2026, Mumbai-born Captain Smit Machchhar was injured after his Omani co-pilot allegedly attacked him aboard a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, but managed to regain control of the aircraft during a mid-air emergency.The two incidents are separated by 40 years, but both involved aviation professionals confronted with moments in which seconds could determine whether hundreds of people survived.Neerja Bhanot: Flight attendant who stayed behindOn September 5, 1986, Pan Am Flight 73 landed at Karachi while operating from Mumbai to New York via Frankfurt. Four armed members of the Abu Nidal Organisation stormed the aircraft and took control of it.Neerja Bhanot, the senior flight purser, was among the first to realise that the aircraft had been hijacked. She alerted the cockpit crew, allowing the pilots to escape and preventing the hijackers from taking the aircraft into the air.When the terrorists ordered the crew to collect passengers' passports, Neerja and other crew members hid the passports of American passengers, whom the hijackers were seeking to identify.The 17-hour standoff ended in gunfire after the hijackers opened fire on passengers. Neerja opened an emergency exit and helped passengers escape through the evacuation chute.She could have escaped herself, but continued helping passengers. She was eventually shot by the hijackers.Over 350 passengers survived the attack, while about 20 people were killed. Neerja was later posthumously awarded the Ashok Chakra, India's highest peacetime gallantry award.The US Department of Justice also honoured her posthumously with its Special Courage Award for 2006.Captain Smit Machchhar: Pilot fighting to keep a jet in airOn Wednesday, the emergency unfolded inside the cockpit of flydubai Flight FZ1073, which was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv with 174 passengers.Captain Smit Machchhar was reportedly attacked and stabbed by his Omani co-pilot, who then apparently tried to crash the jetliner carrying around 170 people. As the confrontation unfolded, the Boeing 737 MAX went into a steep descent.Flight-tracking data showed the aircraft dropping thousands of feet within seconds. One account cited a fall from about 30,875 feet to 16,750 feet in just 29 seconds, with an extreme descent rate of around 30,000 feet per minute.Despite being injured, Machchhar managed to fight back and regain control of the aircraft. Passengers and crew then entered the cockpit and overpowered the attacker.The aircraft was eventually diverted to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia, where it made an emergency landing. The plane had suffered significant damage to its rudder during the extreme descent, according to accounts cited in the material.From a 19-year-old aviation dream to a crisis at 30,000ftMachchhar had not originally planned to become a pilot.In an interview recorded a year before the incident, he said he had initially studied textile engineering and later joined a management course with the intention of helping his family's textile business. It was at an aviation seminar during that course, when he was 19, that he decided to pursue flying.His mother was initially scared by the decision because commercial aviation was far less familiar to people around him at the time.Machchhar went on to build more than 13 years of commercial flying experience on Boeing 737 aircraft. He joined SpiceJet in 2011, later becoming a senior commander and line training captain, before moving to flydubai in June 2022 as a direct-entry captain. His profile lists more than 9,750 flying hours.Two different emergencies, one common threadNeerja and Machchhar faced completely different threats — one a terrorist hijacking, the other a violent cockpit confrontation.But in both cases, the crisis unfolded at close quarters, with the lives of hundreds of passengers depending on decisions made within seconds.Neerja stayed behind to help passengers escape a hijacked aircraft and lost her life in the process. Four decades later, Machchhar was injured while resisting an attack inside the cockpit and helped prevent a plunging aircraft from becoming a catastrophe.Their stories also show two very different forms of aviation bravery: A cabin crew member guiding frightened passengers towards an exit while gunfire erupted around her, and a pilot battling to regain control of a jet that was rapidly losing altitude.In both cases, the people at the centre of the crisis were aviation professionals who found themselves facing extraordinary danger while responsible for the lives of those on board.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Fine call by court
articles.summary: For the nth time, Supreme Court has held a case of preventive detention illegal, and fined, this time, UP govt Rs 10L.
articles.body: For the nth time, Supreme Court has held a case of preventive detention illegal, and fined, this time, UP govt Rs 10L. SC imposed the fine for “blurring…the distinction between punitive and preventive jurisdictions, in substance.” The unfortunate reality is, authorities blur this distinction in a case too many. Special laws such as NSA, PSA, and PMLA make bail tough, where routine criminal law allows bail. Courts have repeatedly held that authorities/ govts can’t keep individuals in lockup/ jail under these laws, where the apparent objective is to ensure undertrials don’t stand a chance at bail. Routine criminal law, allowing bail, would suffice in many of these cases. Courts have held special laws give the executive extraordinary power in stringent provisions, but only within tightly defined boundaries.Allahabad HC had also held govt failed to distinguish between areas of law & order, and public order. If the petitioner was likely to harm law & order only, and not impact public order, then detention under NSA wasn’t legally sustainable. Similarly, J&K quashed a PSA detention last year, because authorities combined two grounds, when the law separates them – acting against security of state, and acting against public order. The difference between law & order, and public order, is not rocket science. What Justice Hidayatullah (Lohia v Bihar 1966) held decades ago bears repeating: “Imagine three concentric circles… ‘Law and order’ represent the largest circle within which is the next circle representing ‘public order’ and the smallest circle represents ‘security of state’… An act may affect law & order, but not public order, just as an act may affect public order, but not security of state.”In case after case, courts have found legal error with preventive detention under special laws. They’ve held that govts stretched their exceptional powers beyond the statute, that requirements for preventive detention weren’t met. That authorities have been fined in such a case is a timely wake-up call.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: Skirting Pak
articles.summary: It’s been over 17 months since Pakistan closed its airspace to Indian airlines, and costs have piled up.
articles.body: It’s been over 17 months since Pakistan closed its airspace to Indian airlines, and costs have piled up. The first 12 months cost Air India alone some 4,000cr. While longer flight durations, extra fuel burn, and staff expenses are a headache, loss of market share to foreign airlines – who aren’t banned over Pakistan – is also a concern now. DGCA’s data for April-June this year shows total passenger volumes to and from India are down 9.1% y-o-y, but foreign airlines’ market share has risen from 53.8% to 62.7%. This can’t go on, and considering how Pakistan has repeatedly shut its airspace to India’s carriers over the years, waiting for it to back off isn’t an option. Instead, viable alternative routes must be found, and Air India, IndiGo, and GOI are already working on it.As TOI reported Wednesday, India is trying to work out a Pakistan bypass via China for its airlines. The proposed route lies over Hotan in northwestern China’s Xinjiang region. While this still involves a detour, it’s not as long as circling Pakistan to get to Europe or North America from airports in Delhi, Amritsar, and Lucknow. And for Central Asian destinations like Tashkent and Almaty, the Hotan route could be as good as flying over Pakistan. Last year, an Indian carrier had suspended flights to these two cities briefly because flight durations had doubled.The other option, as the aviation minister has suggested, is to fly more westward routes out of southern airports that are not affected by the Pakistani airspace closure. With recent improvements in India-China ties – EAM Jaishankar spoke about it in New York on Monday – the Hotan route is possible, and as the aviation minister has said, “Diplomatic level talks are underway.”At a time international air travel growth is averaging 5% annually, Indian carriers can’t be losing market share. But the circumstances are beyond their control. Before the airspace closure, about 20% of their international flights crossed Pakistan. Overnight, flights to the same destinations became 47 minutes longer, on average. And those to San Francisco and Vancouver, for example, became up to four hours longer. This year, Iran war has pushed up jet fuel costs, so Indian carriers are not only flying longer routes, but also paying more per mile. So, foreign airlines – overflying Pakistan as usual – have a huge cost advantage. An alternative route would be a win for Indian business and diplomacy.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: AI could force over 10 million US workers into new careers by 2035: What the McKinsey report underlines
articles.summary: For ages, everyone’s worried AI would come for their jobs. But things aren’t as cut and dried as that old “robots stealing our jobs” story.
articles.body: For ages, everyone’s worried AI would come for their jobs. But things aren’t as cut and dried as that old “robots stealing our jobs” story. The latest report from the McKinsey Global Institute doesn’t predict mass unemployment; it actually paints a messier picture. AI and automation aren’t just threatening to erase jobs. They’re shaking up the work landscape so much that millions of people will have little choice but to switch careers entirely.Here’s the number that may stun you a bit: by 2035, about 11 million Americans, which is nearly 6.5% of the current workforce, may need to leave the fields they’re in and start over in new lines of work. That doesn’t mean 11 million pink slips. McKinsey expects there will likely be even more jobs available than there are now.The real problem here? People need to get from here to there, helping them leave shrinking jobs for ones that are growing.And this is all arriving on top of an already stressed labor market. Job openings dropped in August to their lowest in months, and not many people seem willing or able to quit and try something new. People feel stuck, and now, the ground under them is about to shift even faster as AI accelerates everything.AI could disrupt 36 million jobs: What comes after that?Per CNN, the McKinsey forecast isn’t just about job loss. It’s actually more complex. Their best guess is that automation will decrease demand by an amount equal to about 36 million jobs by 2035. But here’s the twist: that doesn’t mean 36 million people out on the street. Many of those jobs get replaced by new ones.McKinsey anticipates growth in AI-driven sectors and the broader economy will create roughly 40 million fresh jobs over the same time. About 25 million folks affected by automation will probably hang on to their jobs, because the industries they’re in will expand enough to absorb the hit.Still, you’ve got 11 million people who’ll need to reinvent themselves, moving into entirely new roles, industries, or skill sets.It's not about having enough jobs: What is it then?Turns out, it’s about getting people into the right ones.McKinsey sums it up as a “mobility, not scarcity” problem. Meaning, there will be jobs. The real question is: Can people actually get to them? Or are they stuck, missing the right training, or simply unable to move for family or financial reasons?And then there’s the pace. We’re not talking about the slow career changes folks made in past decades. McKinsey figures around 770,000 people every year, for the next decade, will switch occupational fields. That’s more than triple the usual rate.Plus, it’s not always clear-cut job losses or obvious layoffs that’ll force change. AI famously morphs existing jobs. It might not erase your role overnight, but it could nudge you into doing something almost unrecognizable from what you were hired for. McKinsey even says about 70% of US workers are likely to see their day-to-day work reinvented by AI: not replaced, but changed.Picture someone who once spent their day generating reports now focusing on checking what AI systems spit out, interpreting that data, handling various tasks, or dealing more directly with customers. So rather than outright destruction, AI keeps reshaping roles in subtle but significant ways.Not everyone gets hit equallyHere’s another layer that adds to the complexity: some workers are at higher risk than others. Jobs with repetitive, predictable, or highly digital routines, like basic data entry or transactional work, have the biggest targets on their backs. On the flip side, there’s massive demand coming for people who know how to develop, run, and keep AI systems in check.And it’s not just about AI. The US is aging, and that’s about to turbocharge hiring for healthcare, at-home support, and long-term care. Demographic changes alone could create eight million new roles, according to McKinsey. Healthcare and social services are already projected to boom, while computer and mathematical roles should see strong growth: 7.3% over a decade, says the US Bureau of Labor Statistics.This means the “AI destroys jobs” panic doesn’t quite fit. There’ll be jobs; just not always the same ones, or in the same places, or for people with the same skills.Moving workers is the hard partThis mess puts the focus on something less exciting than robots: retraining. McKinsey expects up to 16 million newly created jobs over the next decade will demand candidates from outside their old fields, meaning experience in that area alone won’t cut it. So even with plenty of opportunities, the real challenge is helping people get the right training, support, and confidence to make big leaps.And lots of Americans already feel penned in. According to the CNN report, weak hiring and low turnover have created a sense of being “stuck.”However, McKinsey isn’t saying millions will simply be tossed aside because of AI. Their warning is more nuanced, and frankly, more urgent: the jobs of 2035 are coming, but today’s workers might not be ready, willing, or able to fill them. That’s a setup for one of the biggest, fastest career reshuffles the country has ever seen: not a jobs apocalypse, but a labor market earthquake that could leave a lot of folks scrambling to keep up.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: 3 accidents a day, but just 8 cashless claims a month: Where's relief scheme going wrong?
articles.summary: GHAZIABAD: Ghaziabad reported an average of three accidents every day in the first four months of the year, but only 40 claims have been received under
articles.body: GHAZIABAD: Ghaziabad reported an average of three accidents every day in the first four months of the year, but only 40 claims have been received under the Centre's PM-Rahat scheme, which provides up to Rs 1.5 lakh in cashless treatment for accident victims, in the five months since it was operationalised in May, averaging eight claims a month.The number points to shortcomings in the way the scheme is being implemented, which assume significance after a 24-year-old accident victim who was seriously injured in a road accident and could not get the level of treatment he needed at a PM Rahat empanelled hospital, died this week.Tushar Kumar's father has alleged his son lost vital time because of a delay in treatment. Tushar was taken to a second hospital, Yashoda Medicity, which is not empanelled and where the father claimed he was asked to clear a bill of Rs 48,000 for Tushar to be released so that he could be moved to Safdarjung Hospital in Delhi.Gautam Budh Nagar's PM- Rahat claims are higher at 149 in the same period (an average of 30 a month), but still very low when compared to accident numbers. According to traffic police data, the city recorded 577 road accidents between Jan and July this year, claiming 450 lives.Officials said a mix of low public and institutional awareness, procedural bottlenecks and uneven hospital empanelment were coming in the way of the ultimate intention - of saving accident victims' lives within the golden hour.What is the scheme?The PM Road Accident Victims' Hospitalisation and Assured Treatment scheme was notified by the highways ministry to ensure that financial constraints do not delay emergency treatment for anyone during the crucial 60 minutes - also referred to as the "golden hour" - immediately following a traumatic injury, when prompt medical and surgical treatment gives the highest likelihood of saving a life.It covers motor vehicle accidents on any category of road and provides cashless treatment of up to Rs 1.5 lakh per road accident victim for a maximum of seven days from the date of the accident. Much of the network of hospitals under the scheme has been built around hospitals already empanelled under Ayushman Bharat scheme.According to official guidelines from Ministry of Road Transport & Highways, the scheme automatically covers all 36,112 hospitals empanelled under Ayushman Bharat (PM-JAY). In Noida, the scheme covers all 61 hospitals under Ayushman Bharat, while in Ghaziabad 86 are empanelled. Health officials told TOI all AB-PMJAY empanelled hospitals that provide the requisite trauma, polytrauma and stabilisation services in compliance with National Health Authority (NHA) guidelines are deemed designated hospitals for cashless road accident treatment.How to avail scheme?The process is designed so that victims or their families do not have to arrange money or complete lengthy paperwork before emergency treatment begins. A victim, bystander or family member can call Dial 112, the emergency response support system, which is integrated with PM-Rahat and can provide ambulance assistance and information about the nearest empanelled hospital. Police responding to an accident can also access the list of empanelled hospitals.Once the victim reaches a designated hospital, treatment begins under the approved health benefit packages. The hospital generates a treatment ID on the NHA's transaction management system (TMS) and sends details to police through the electronic detailed accident report (eDAR) system for verification.Police authentication runs alongside treatment and is not a prerequisite for the hospital to begin emergency care. Police have up to 24 hours to respond through eDAR, or up to 48 hours in cases the hospital administrator classifies as life-threatening. The system creates a digital trail from the accident report through admission, treatment, police verification, claim processing and payment.Who can avail scheme?Officials said the scheme is not restricted to people who hold an Ayushman Bharat card. PM-Rahat is a separate statutory scheme for victims of road accidents involving motor vehicles, and it covers people irrespective of the insurance status, with the reimbursement mechanism varying by circumstances. "At the time of billing, if a patient has Ayushman Bharat, or any other private insurance, they can avail those. However, if one does not have any insurance, then the PM-Rahat scheme can be used," the official said.Ghaziabad health department nodal officer (road safety) Dr Pankaj Rakesh said the district had taken steps to ensure that police and emergency responders know where designated hospitals are located. "Information about the empanelled hospitals, including their names and locations, has been shared with police officials at different levels, including police stations and senior officers, as well as emergency service providers. The objective is to ensure that once an accident is reported, the responding personnel can quickly identify the nearest PM-Rahat empanelled hospital and arrange for the victim to be shifted there without losing critical time," Rakesh said.He added that lists of empanelled hospitals were also being made available at key points on the highway network.Denial of admission or treatment under PM-Rahat amounts to non-compliance with the scheme and can attract punitive measures under the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010, or the corresponding state-specific laws.States and UTs can take action under applicable laws, while the empanelment framework also provides for disciplinary action, suspension and de-empanelment.Why uptake is low?Strict digital deadlines, patchy hospital empanelment and early-stage system gaps have affected the uptake and reimbursement process. A victim can become ineligible for the scheme's benefits if hospitalisation occurs more than 24 hours after an accident. Police also need to authenticate claims within 24 hours for non-life-threatening injuries and 48 hours for life-threatening ones, or an application can be rejected. Some empanelled hospitals still turn patients away or demand upfront payment, fearing delayed reimbursement. According to health department data, 679 claims were approved since rollout, while 168 were rejected after no response was received from the police within the prescribed timelines. Another 40 life-threatening cases were found ineligible under the scheme by the police. Under the scheme, cases classified as life-threatening by the hospital administration remain eligible for treatment until the case is rejected by the police through e-DAR or until 48 hours have elapsed, whichever is earlier.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Ghaziabad | Silver Rate in Ghaziabad | Bank Holidays in Ghaziabad | Public Holidays in Ghaziabad | Ghaziabad AQI | Weather in Ghaziabad | Petrol Price in Ghaziabad | Diesel Price in Ghaziabad | CNG Price in Ghaziabad | LPG Price in GhaziabadStay updated with the latest Ghaziabad news.
